strengths: Clear identification and formalization of an under-explored failure mode (semantic collapsing) in generative personalization with well-motivated concrete examples
Comprehensive empirical analysis using multiple distance metrics (L2, Hausdorff, Mahalanobis, KL divergence) in both textual and image spaces, with consistent findings across methods (TI, DB, CD)
Root cause analysis convincingly demonstrates that unconstrained optimization leads to embedding drift in both magnitude and direction, with clear visualization of the phenomenon
Practical, lightweight solution that is training-free, post-hoc applicable, and compatible with multiple existing personalization methods
Nuanced understanding that SCP has both negative and positive effects depending on prompt type, demonstrating sophistication beyond binary problem-solution framing
Thorough hyperparameter analysis and ablation studies showing effects of α and β across diverse concepts and datasets
weaknesses: Solution novelty is limited—SLERP interpolation is a straightforward, relatively obvious approach once the problem is identified; lacks comparison with alternative solutions (training-time regularization, linear interpolation, orthogonal constraints)
Incomplete theoretical understanding: paper demonstrates that semantic drift occurs but lacks deep insight into why it happens during personalization or why SLERP is theoretically optimal

Significant evaluation limitations: single base model (SD v1.5) with no validation on newer models (SDXL, SD 2.0); entirely automatic metrics with no human evaluation despite CLIP's known biases; unclear definition of 'ground truth image'

Substantial trade-offs inadequately addressed: improving prompt alignment (CLIPf_T) often sacrifices visual fidelity (CLIP-I drops by 2-4 points in Tables 6-7), but this fundamental trade-off is underexplored

Hyperparameter selection lacks principled methodology: despite claims of 'easily chosen' parameters, Table 1 shows α is sensitive; β=1.5 is ad-hoc with no justification for the specific interpolation formula

Limited scope: only single-concept and exploratory multi-concept analysis without proposed solutions; findings generalization to different concept types, reference set sizes, and training durations unclear
Multi-concept analysis (Section 3.3) identifies the problem but provides no solution, making this contribution incomplete and disconnected from main narrative

Missing key comparisons: no comparison with concurrent regularization approaches (e.g., orthogonal finetuning [21]), no ablation of SLERP vs. alternatives, no comparison with other post-hoc adjustment methods
Experimental design choices not validated: 200 contextual prompts via LLM selected arbitrarily without sensitivity analysis; construction of P_V*, P_c, P^simple may introduce LLM-specific biases

Insufficient reproducibility: LLM specification for prompt generation missing, computational cost not analyzed, statistical significance testing absent despite sample size variability across experiments

strengths: Clear problem formulation: Articulates well-motivated Semantic Collapsing Problem distinct from language drift with clear problem statement and motivation
Comprehensive empirical analysis: Multiple distance metrics, analysis in both textual and image spaces, visualization across methods (TI, DB, CD), and systematic investigation
Root cause identification: Links SCP to unconstrained optimization with clear evidence (Figure 4) showing embedding norm growth and direction drift
Practical applicability: Training-free, test-time only method that works post-hoc across multiple personalization methods
Thorough experimental setup: Good use of diverse prompts, multiple datasets (CustomConcept101, CelebA-HQ), and extensive ablations on hyperparameters
weaknesses: Limited solution novelty: SLERP interpolation is straightforward and well-established; lacks technical depth and no comparison with alternative approaches (linear interpolation, other geometric methods)

Modest and inconsistent improvements: Table 6 shows gains of 0.34-1.87 in CLIPf_T with significant trade-offs (e.g., TI+TEA: -2.34 in CLIP-I); many improvements within standard deviation with no statistical significance testing

Hyperparameter sensitivity undermines universality claims: α significantly impacts performance (6.4% CLIPf_T variation in Table 1); fixed α=0.2, β=1.5 acknowledged as suboptimal; contradicts training-free and broadly applicable framing
Unresolved fundamental trade-off: Paper identifies but doesn't solve the semantic alignment vs. visual fidelity trade-off; fixed hyperparameters represent arbitrary compromise without user control

Limited experimental validation: Only Stable Diffusion v1.5 evaluated (not SDXL or SD 2.0); no comparison with training-time regularization approaches; no user studies; multi-concept analysis uses only one concept pair

Methodological issues: Arbitrary prompt segmentation without justification; over-reliance on CLIP-based metrics without addressing known limitations; token-by-token SLERP in Equation 2 lacks justification; missing ablations on interpolation method choice
Two-way impact finding inadequately addressed: Section 3.2.2 shows SCP sometimes beneficial, yet solution treats uniformly; suggests problem is more nuanced than presented but complexity not resolved

Reproducibility concerns: Code availability unclear; hyperparameter choices unexplained (e.g., β=1.5 formula); synthetic prompt generation details incomplete; limited implementation details for DreamBooth variant
Scope limitations: Only text-to-image personalization; limited concept types (faces, objects); unclear generalization to other domains; no evaluation on newer diffusion models or other T2I systems

Unclear practical significance: No analysis of whether improvements are perceptually meaningful; visual results (Figures 16-17) show modest improvements not always obvious; no justification for which improvement metric matters most

strengths: Clear identification and formalization of the semantic collapsing problem (SCP), distinct from language drift, addressing an under-explored failure mode in generative personalization
Comprehensive empirical analysis with rigorous evaluation across multiple distance metrics (L2, Hausdorff, Mahalanobis, KL divergence) and multiple personalization methods (TI, DB, CD)
Nuanced insights into two-way impacts of SCP: negative effects on complex prompt alignment and positive effects when subjects require strong visual presence
Practical, training-free test-time solution (SLERP-based embedding adjustment) broadly applicable across different personalization methods without retraining
Thorough experimental evaluation including hyperparameter analysis, consistent improvements across diverse concepts, and detailed qualitative results
Extension to multi-concept scenarios demonstrates understanding of more complex, realistic personalization settings
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty of proposed solution—SLERP interpolation is straightforward; no ablation on alternative interpolation methods or justification for SLERP specifically
Modest empirical improvements with concerning trade-offs: TI+TEA gains 0.54-0.64 CLIP_T points; DB+TEA on CelebA shows -4.55 CLIP-I drop; improvements inconsistent across methods
Unresolved hyperparameter trade-offs requiring manual selection (α=0.2, β=1.5); increasing α improves prompt alignment (CLIPf_T) but decreases visual fidelity (CLIP-I from 73.5 to 63.6)
Root cause (unconstrained optimization) identified but only addressed via test-time adjustment; no exploration of training-time regularization solutions or fundamental fixes
Multi-concept personalization analysis (Section 3.3) shows SCP intensifies but provides no evidence that TEA mitigates this problem, limiting practical applicability

Limited evaluation scope: tested only on Stable Diffusion v1.5, not on newer/larger models (SDXL, SD 2.0); no user studies despite quality improvement claims; LLM-generated contextual prompts may not reflect real usage patterns

Methodological clarity issues: unclear how token-level adjustment (Eq. 1) informs prompt-level adjustment (Eq. 2) for DreamBooth; target concept c selection criteria not fully specified; prompt construction methodology underspecified
Evaluation focused on complex prompts where SCP is problematic; acknowledged two-way impact suggests method could harm simple prompts, but limited analysis of when TEA is beneficial vs. harmful

strengths: Clear identification and empirical demonstration of the Semantic Collapsing Problem (SCP), a previously under-explored issue in generative personalization with strong evidence across multiple domains

Practical test-time solution (TEA) that is training-free, broadly compatible with existing personalization methods (Textual Inversion, DreamBooth, CustomDiffusion, etc.), and requires no model retraining
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple methods, datasets, and metrics with consistent improvements demonstrated in both quantitative metrics and qualitative results
Thorough investigation of root causes using embedding norm distributions, multiple distance metrics, and multi-concept analysis to characterize the phenomenon
Extensive ablation studies systematically analyzing hyperparameter sensitivity and robustness across different settings
Novel secondary finding revealing a vulnerability in Anti-DreamBooth privacy defenses, suggesting broader implications beyond personalization
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the proposed solution (SLERP interpolation) is straightforward and represents an incremental contribution without significant algorithmic innovation

Incomplete theoretical understanding: no mechanistic explanation for why SLERP specifically addresses SCP, why this interpolation method is chosen over alternatives, or why training-time constraints weren't explored

Hyperparameter dependency undermines generalizability: σ and β require tuning across different prompts/datasets (Figures 12-13), and no principled strategy is provided for selecting hyperparameters for new domains
Insufficient evaluation rigor: lacks error bars, confidence intervals, statistical significance testing, and user studies to validate perceived improvements in semantic fidelity
Limited evaluation scope: uses only 9 concepts from CustomConcept101 and 10 subjects from CelebA; no cross-domain or large-scale evaluation
Missing comparisons with alternatives: no systematic comparison with training-time constraint approaches, other embedding adjustment methods, or alternative interpolation strategies
Incomplete trade-off analysis: shows visual-fidelity vs prompt-consistency trade-offs (Figures 22-23) but lacks systematic quantitative analysis of performance degradation in different dimensions
Ethical concerns inadequately addressed: application to circumvent privacy defenses is concerning, but limited discussion of improved defenses or misuse implications
Presentation clarity: dense notation with multiple abbreviations and key results relegated to appendices make the paper difficult to follow
